1.pericope_label: The third coming and the rule of witnesses

schools.summary: Gill offers two reckonings of the visits and counts the admonitions as the witnesses; Calvin makes the three approaches stand in the place of three witnesses by accommodation, and defends naming notorious offenders in public.
Henry takes the two epistles for the witnesses and refers the rule to Christ’s directions rather than to the law of Moses, adding that the account Paul kept is also kept in heaven.

Barnes argues from "the second time" that Paul had been at Corinth only once; Ellicott weighs three visits against one visit, one abandoned purpose and one intention, prefers the latter, and attacks the reading that makes Paul’s comings themselves the witnesses; Robertson leaves the grammar undecided.

Clarke reports and rejects the case for an unrecorded second visit and takes the threatened punishment as a real power to inflict bodily harm; Wesley holds that the earlier comings were intended rather than made.
Chrysostom sees Paul joining the unwritten to the written, putting his comings and warnings in the place of witnesses, and praises a discipline that warns often and punishes late in imitation of God.

debates: How many times Paul had actually visited Corinth, where Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott argue for one previous visit, an earlier authority Clarke quotes argues for two, and Robertson holds the grammar to be indecisive.
Whether the two or three witnesses are Paul’s own comings and warnings (Chrysostom, Calvin, Henry, Gill) or the ordinary legal rule applied to the inquiry he will hold (Ellicott, Barnes, Robertson).
outliers: Ellicott calls the accommodated reading of the witnesses strained and almost fantastic and raises a fatal objection to it, without acknowledging that Chrysostom and Calvin hold it in the same collection.
Calvin turns the passage into a rule for pastoral discipline, permitting public reproof only where the offence is already notorious.

3.pericope_label: The proof of Christ speaking in Paul, and the weakness of the cross

schools.summary: Gill makes the Corinthians themselves the seal of Paul’s apostleship and holds that Christ could have prevented the crucifixion as God; Calvin reads the challenge as an injury to Christ, lays down that any teacher’s doctrine may be examined until Christ has manifested Himself in him, and warns against extending Christ’s voluntary suffering into a denial that his humanity was truly mortal.

Barnes finds the proof in the punishment itself and refers Christ’s power toward them to calamities already suffered, explaining the weakness as a real human sensibility to suffering; Ellicott prefers the shorter reading of the verse and refers "we shall live with him" to present spiritual power rather than to the resurrection; Robertson simply expects the proof to be given.

Clarke points to their conversion as the proof and stresses that none could take Christ’s life from him; Wesley refers the promised life to being raised from the dead and the power of God to the energy now at work in believers.

debates: Whether Christ’s death followed from a nature genuinely liable to death or only from a voluntary permission over a nature not properly mortal, Calvin arguing the first against a version of the second that Gill and Clarke both press.
Whether "we shall live with him" means present spiritual power (Ellicott) or the future resurrection (Wesley).
What "not weak toward you" refers to: miracles and the force of the gospel, or the punitive calamities Barnes prefers.
outliers: Calvin uses the verse to defend the examination of every teacher’s doctrine, including one who claims to speak with Christ’s authority.
Ellicott notes that the better manuscripts omit the concessive clause, giving "for even He was crucified".

5.pericope_label: Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith

schools.summary: Gill distinguishes standing in the doctrine of faith from possessing the grace of faith; Calvin argues that the one Christ dwelling in the people cannot be denied in the minister, draws from this the dependence of faith on preaching, and uses the verse to defend the assurance of faith against those who allow only a moral conjecture.

Ellicott places the emphasis on "yourselves" and turns the demand for proof back on the Corinthians, defining "reprobate" as failing the scrutiny and denying that later Calvinist senses belong to it; Barnes distinguishes the two verbs and insists proof is made in living rather than in reflection; Robertson notes that this is the word Paul feared for himself.

Clarke reads the whole passage through the assaying of adulterated coin and holds that the only reprobation in view is self-incurred; Wesley defines the word as inability to bear the test and reports a rendering that puts Christ among the church rather than within each believer.

debates: What "reprobate" means here: failure to pass a test, with Clarke, Wesley and Ellicott all excluding any doctrine of decreed rejection, and Ellicott naming Calvinist theology as the source of the intrusion, while Calvin on the same verse is defending assurance and does not engage the question.
Whether "Christ is in you" is said of each believer or of the church corporately, a rendering Wesley reports without adopting.
outliers: Barnes proves the point with an axe: its quality is learned in the woods, not by inspection or reading.
Calvin makes the congregation’s own faith the minister’s only well grounded credential.

7.pericope_label: The prayer that they do no evil, and the wish for their restoration

schools.summary: Gill notes the better reading "we pray" and holds that apostolic authority was never meant for those who walk in the truth; Calvin makes the pastor’s indifference to his own reputation a rule of ministry, limits the power of church officers to the service of the truth against those who claim unbounded dominion, and reads the closing word as the sound proportion of all the members.
Henry makes the petition a model of intercession and insists that power given for edification cannot be turned to destruction.

Barnes reads the verse as softening the previous threat and takes the maxim about the truth as a guarantee of apostolic integrity; Ellicott finds under it the condition on which the power is held, and renders the closing word "restoration"; Robertson takes the maxim generally, that the truth wins in the long run.

Clarke records an alternative construal in which Paul prays not to be forced to use the rod, and expounds the closing word as the setting of a dislocated limb and the ordering of a building; Wesley keeps to the plain sense and defines perfection as the faith that works by love.

debates: What "we can do nothing against the truth" asserts: the integrity of apostolic teaching and discipline (Barnes, Clarke), the condition limiting the exercise of apostolic power (Ellicott, Gill), the bounds set to all church authority (Calvin, Henry), or a general maxim that truth prevails in the end (Robertson).
Whether the prayer asks that the Corinthians do no evil or that Paul be spared having to do them harm, an alternative Clarke reports.
outliers: Calvin turns the verse against those who cite Christ’s "he that heareth you heareth me" to claim unlimited authority, answering that rulers in the Church are themselves subject to the truth.
Ellicott compares Paul’s willingness to seem a failure with the wish to be accursed for his brethren and with the Baptist’s consent to decrease.

10.pericope_label: Written while absent, that he need not be sharp when present

schools.summary: Gill reads the verse as summarising Paul’s whole purpose in writing; Calvin holds that the threat is armed with God’s authority rather than personal passion, distinguishes this use of edification from the earlier one, and argues that authority turning to a hearer’s condemnation acts against its own nature.

Barnes treats the verse as an apology meant to forestall severe measures; Ellicott hears love winning an inner conflict and insists that even action would have aimed at restoration rather than display; Robertson glosses the rare adverb for sharpness as a cutting off.
Clarke renders the word as a cutting off and stresses that the power was given for edification rather than destruction.

Chrysostom collects the severe passages of the letter and has Paul wish the sharpness to stay in the writing and never pass into deeds, while noting that the threat is armed with the Lord’s authority and that punishing the unamended would itself be a building up.

debates: Whether punishment can itself be edification: Chrysostom concludes that chastising the unrepentant is a building up, while Calvin holds that any turn toward destruction is contrary to the nature of the power given.
outliers: Chrysostom states the apostle’s wish as a preference that his threats remain threats and never be carried out.
Calvin takes the verse as fixing the limit of pastoral power for all ministers, not only for Paul.

11.pericope_label: Finally, brethren, farewell: the closing exhortations

schools.summary: Gill takes the farewell as a call to spiritual joy in Christ; Calvin distinguishes unity of sentiment from union of hearts, warns that where strife reigns the devil reigns, and observes that Paul softens the ending so as not to leave the church exasperated.

Henry urges one mind where it can be had and peace where it cannot, so that difference of judgment need not alienate affection, and rests the exhortation on the promise that the God of love and peace dwells with the peaceable.

Barnes and Ellicott both explain the greeting as the ordinary word for rejoicing, Ellicott making consolation the keynote of the epistle and referring the call to unity back to the Corinthian schisms, while Barnes uses "be perfect" to challenge the doctrine of sinless perfection to produce a single instance.

Clarke gives the English word its etymology, reads "be perfect" as getting back into joint, and takes the next command as admonition received in order that comfort may follow; Wesley reads the same word as aspiring to the highest degree of holiness.

debates: What "be perfect" requires: restoration of a dislocated body to order (Clarke, Ellicott, Barnes) or the pursuit of the highest holiness (Wesley) — with Barnes in the same chapter demanding that any claim of sinless perfection produce one example, and Wesley making no answer.
Whether the following command means to be comforted, to comfort one another, or to receive admonition, where Barnes, Ellicott and Clarke each take a different option.
outliers: Barnes and Clarke independently close their comment on the farewell with the same remark about the dying words of Cyrus.
Clarke concludes that where neither peace nor love is present God is absent and the assembly consists of the congregation and the devil.

12.pericope_label: The holy kiss and the greeting of the saints

schools.summary: Gill grounds the mutual greeting in what all the saints share: the same favour, the same redeeming blood and the same sanctifying grace.

Ellicott reads the command as directing a single act at the close of the reading and traces the kiss through the Eastern and Western liturgies to its suppression and replacement by a kissing tablet; Robertson gives the same history from the synagogue practice forward, noting its survival in the Coptic and Russian churches and its abandonment under pagan slander; Barnes places the writing of the letter in Macedonia.
Clarke takes the kiss as practical counsel toward a good understanding and observes that in the primitive church a saint and a Christian were one and the same.

outliers: Ellicott and Robertson independently trace the same later history of the kiss, including its replacement by a tablet passed from hand to hand, Robertson dating the English innovation to the middle of the thirteenth century.
Ellicott draws from the greeting Paul’s habit of telling one church that he was writing to another.

schools.summary: Calvin answers the objection that the love of God should have preceded the grace of Christ by distinguishing what is true when we look at God from what is true when we look at ourselves; Gill takes the grace of Christ either for his eternal love or for the fulness lodged in him as Mediator.
Henry takes the verse as an acknowledgment of three distinct persons in one God and as the proper dismissal of a worshipping assembly.

Ellicott traces the benediction into the Eastern liturgies and the English Prayer Book and explains the inverted order of the divine names by the sequence of Paul’s thought; Barnes argues from the prayer that worship may be offered to the Son and the Spirit, that the divine nature admits a real distinction, and that the Spirit is a person rather than an attribute; Robertson calls it the fullest of the benedictions and reports that the letter achieved its purpose.

Clarke expounds each divine title, then turns the word for fellowship into an argument that a believer may be as sure of his acceptance as of his own existence, and calls any teaching that allows endless doubt a spurious gospel; Wesley glosses the three clauses and rebukes those who leave before the blessing is finished.
Cyril of Jerusalem cites the benediction at the close of a catalogue of texts marshalled to prove that the Holy Spirit subsists, lives, speaks and foretells.

debates: Why the Son is named before the Father, where Ellicott finds the order settled by the sequence of thought and Calvin by the difference between viewing salvation from God’s side and from ours.
How far assurance extends, Clarke holding that a believer may know his acceptance as certainly as his own existence and condemning any doctrine that leaves it uncertain.
outliers: Ellicott dismisses the subscription naming Philippi as the addition of an unknown transcriber, while allowing that it is probably a fair inference.
Wesley turns the benediction into a rebuke of congregations that disperse before it is pronounced.
